claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 5, and 6, run a preregistered realistic editing benchmark comparing ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and ordinary fine-tuning on publicly available GPT-2-XL and GPT-J-6B checkpoints. Draw validated, nontrivial edits from the Hugging Face versions of COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, excluding facts the base model cannot recall, and apply 1, 10, 100, and 1000 edits both in batches and sequentially without rollback. After each edit count, measure reliability on canonical prompts, generalization on paraphrases, COUNTERFACT ES/PS/NS, portability on reversed and one-hop queries, and locality on relation-matched and random out-of-scope prompts. Measure broader damage using publicly available HellaSwag, LAMBADA, Natural Questions, held-out factual recall, perplexity, and generation consistency. Use multiple random edit orders and bootstrap confidence intervals, preserve all intermediate checkpoints, and include the unedited model and edit-by-edit rollback as controls. Near-perfect prior results would fail realistic evaluation if high single-edit efficacy falls materially under paraphrases, portability tests, or cumulative editing, or if it coincides with statistically and practically significant losses in locality or core-task performance. Stable efficacy and generalization through 1000 edits with negligible capability loss across models and datasets would refute or sharply limit the claim; monotonic or superlinear degradation with edit count would support compounding and global propagation. This experiment could be unnecessary if prior work released complete no-rollback checkpoints and per-edit evaluations across these datasets, models, and capability controls, permitting an equivalent independent reanalysis.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, test whether edit damage is caused by amplification along low-variance representation directions. For each model, layer, and subject-token position, estimate the pre-edit activation covariance spectrum from a large public text sample such as WikiText-103, plus unrelated COUNTERFACT and ZSRE prompts. Apply ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and matched-norm fine-tuning edits, then decompose both the parameter-induced activation displacement and downstream logit displacement into covariance eigen-directions. Test whether amplification, defined as downstream change per unit edit projection, increases as pre-edit variance decreases, using regressions that control for layer, edit norm, relation, token position, and immediate edit efficacy. Measure propagation by tracing displacement through later layers and by counting significant output-distribution changes over thousands of unrelated prompts. For a causal test, construct matched interventions that preserve update norm and canonical-prompt efficacy but either project the update away from the lowest-variance subspace, into it, or rotate it within the same layer; repeat across layers and validate localization with both causal tracing under several corruption magnitudes and representation zeroing. The geometric account is supported if low-variance projection predicts global change across algorithms and backbones, deliberately increasing that projection increases collateral damage, and removing it reduces damage without eliminating edit efficacy. A correlation that disappears after controlling for layer or edit norm, or failure of the projection intervention to alter damage, would favor incidental algorithmic or layer-selection explanations. This experiment could be omitted if existing work provides activations, edit deltas, covariance decompositions, and norm- and efficacy-matched projection interventions across multiple editors and backbones.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, compare strict weight-preserving editing with parameter editing under a common end-to-end utility and resource budget. Implement an IKE-style retrieval-and-prompt memory that stores each COUNTERFACT or ZSRE correction externally and automatically retrieves it at inference time; cryptographically hash every base-model tensor before and after editing and audit the optimizer state to verify that no model weight changed. Compare it against ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, a prompt containing the fact without retrieval, and a retrieval system containing irrelevant or shuffled facts. Evaluate the same 1, 10, 100, and 1000-edit streams on reliability, paraphrase generalization, locality, one-hop portability, and core capabilities, while also reporting retrieval failures, latency, context-token cost, external-memory size, and edited or added parameter counts. Use GPT-2-XL and GPT-J-6B and public COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions data, with matched edit sets and repeated retrieval-index seeds. The approach is a serious alternative if it lies on or dominates the Pareto frontier of factual accuracy, locality, cumulative stability, latency, and memory, particularly if it remains reversible and stable at large edit counts; it is merely a fallback if it succeeds only when the exact correction is retrieved, fails paraphrases or reasoning transfer, or incurs prohibitive inference costs relative to a weight editor with comparable safety. Unchanged hashes establish only that base weights remain untouched, not that the overall system is parameter-free if a trainable retriever or adapter is added, so both strict no-trained-component and frozen-base-with-extra-component results should be reported separately. This experiment could be unnecessary if reproducible systems already expose tensor hashes, external-memory contents, and matched accuracy, locality, latency, and scaling measurements against current weight editors.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An uncontaminated pre-edit baseline and a single-edit comparison using ordinary generated inference rather than answer-token assistance, so apparent near-perfect efficacy can be separated from protocol-induced inflation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 includes an unedited control, explicitly evaluates the one-edit condition, and uses end-to-end generated responses in a preregistered realistic benchmark rather than supplying target answers. It therefore gives both the clean floor and an honest comparison against prior near-perfect results.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A scoring validation that checks semantic judgments across reliability, generalization, locality, and portability against an independent deterministic token-level measure, so method rankings cannot be attributed to evaluator subjectivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures the relevant editing dimensions and includes deterministic-looking edit metrics such as ES/PS/NS, but it does not require a semantic judge and an independent token-level cross-check of the same outcomes. The resulting numbers can be compared, but agreement or disagreement between evaluator-dependent semantic quality and deterministic matching would remain unresolved.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment establishes whether the reported method ranking survives an independent, deterministic scoring instrument rather than being an artifact of a semantic evaluator.
The proposed benchmark specifies several outcome dimensions and edit metrics, but does not specify both semantic judging and a matched token-level validation for those dimensions.
Consequently, a judge-induced ranking or a disagreement between semantic adequacy and token matching could persist without being diagnosed.
The team would fail to learn whether its editing-method conclusions are robust to the scoring instrument; partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, normalized, direction-resolved test of whether edit-induced representation changes are disproportionately amplified in low-variance directions and whether the pattern is reproducible across editing methods, layers, model backbones, and cumulative edits.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 directly estimates the covariance spectrum, decomposes activation and logit displacement into its eigen-directions, controls for important confounds, and adds norm- and efficacy-matched interventions that project updates into or away from low-variance subspaces. Proposed experiment 0 supplies repeated sequential edit counts and tests monotonic or superlinear cumulative damage. Together they provide the directional mechanism test and its accumulation behavior without requiring the reference statistic itself.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A broad head-to-head evaluation of representative parameter-modifying and weight-preserving editing families across large-model backbones, fact collections, edit loads, and efficacy and side-effect dimensions, including sequential accumulation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 compares multiple parameter-modifying families on two large-model backbones and two factual-edit collections at one through 1000 edits, in both batch and sequential modes, while measuring reliability, generalization, portability, locality, and broader utility. Proposed experiment 2 adds a retrieval-and-prompt, weight-preserving comparator on matched streams and the same utility dimensions. This is sufficient comparative scope for the claim; the reference's exact method count, named checkpoints, and exact edit-count endpoint are not binding.

evidence.quote: We explore whether ICL can edit factual knowledge. To answer the question, we give a comprehensive empirical study of ICL strategies. Experiments show that in-context knowledge editing (IKE), without any gradient and parameter updating, achieves a competitive success rate compared to gradient-based methods on GPT-J (6B) but with much fewer side effects
evidence.bearing: Supports treating a weight-preserving retrieval/in-context editor as a substantive comparator for parameter editing, rather than as an unrelated baseline.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An out-of-target capability evaluation after sequential edits on independent reasoning and broad knowledge tasks, allowing loss of core capabilities to be distinguished from mere failure to implant the requested facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 evaluates broader capabilities, held-out factual recall, perplexity, and generation consistency at the same cumulative edit loads, including 10 and 100 sequential edits. Proposed experiment 2 repeats the matched utility comparison for the weight-preserving alternative. Different capability suites are acceptable here because the claim requires evidence of untargeted capability damage, not the particular named benchmarks used in the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Robustness and boundary evidence testing whether the conclusion persists across model scale, knowledge structures and fact difficulty, and sensitive or exceptional editor configurations rather than being an artifact of one setup.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set varies model backbone, factual collection, editing algorithm, edit order, and edit count, and the mechanism study uses matched-norm and projection interventions. However, it does not test a larger model scale, a distinct event-level knowledge representation, explicit high- versus low-confidence fact strata, or the configuration and failure modes of a potentially non-collapsing editor. Thus it gives some robustness evidence but leaves the most important scope and exception questions ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes a general limitation from one caused by model scale, fact representation or difficulty, or an exceptional method configuration.
The proposed set varies two backbones, two factual collections, several methods, and edit streams, so it does test some transfer beyond a single setup.
It does not include larger-scale models, event-level facts, explicit confidence/difficulty strata, or sensitivity analysis of an editor that might escape collapse.
Therefore a stable or unstable result on the proposed set cannot tell whether the conclusion changes on those omitted scales, knowledge types, fact subsets, or exception configurations.
The team would fail to learn whether the claimed limitation is bounded to the tested scope or survives those key robustness and exception tests; partial.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests realistic cumulative editing and untargeted damage, performs a substantially stronger causal geometric analysis than a simple observational correlation, and verifies the weight-preserving comparator's unchanged tensors while comparing end-to-end utility and resource costs. Those outcomes would address the central claim for the tested backbones and edit distributions. The claim would not be fully settled as written because the proposed scoring protocol does not independently validate semantic rankings against deterministic token-level scoring, and the robustness sweep omits larger scales, event-level knowledge, explicit difficulty strata, and sensitivity testing of an exceptional editor.
missing: An independent semantic-versus-deterministic scoring cross-check on the same reliability, generalization, locality, and portability outcomes.

A scope and exception sweep over larger model scales, distinct event-level knowledge, explicit fact-confidence/difficulty strata, and a parameter editor/configuration that may not collapse, including its sensitivity analysis.
